Am I required to carry it?

Whether you must carry it depends on your exact address and loan — look your address up on FEMA's flood map. If the building is in a high-risk zone (any zone starting with A or V, such as A, AE, AH, AO or VE) and the loan comes from a federally regulated or insured lender, the law requires it. For context, 61.9% of Harrison County's existing NFIP policies sit in those high-risk zones — not 61.9% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home.

Policies by rated zone (summed policyCount; condo buildings count each unit). Federal rule (42 U.S.C. §4012a): coverage is required on a building in a Special Flood Hazard Area when the loan comes from a federally regulated lender or the purchase or construction gets federal financial assistance. A lender can require it in any zone.

How much does it cost here?

Among existing single-family primary-residence NFIP policies in Harrison County, the median annual cost is $1,212, with the middle half between $991 and $1,551 (7,700 policies). This is what current policyholders pay — a new policy on a different building can differ. How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Flood damage is almost never covered by a standard homeowners policy; you buy flood insurance separately through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Two facts change your timing and your limits:

  • Waiting period~30 days
  • If your lender requires it at closingNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most NFIP policies take effect 30 days after you buy, so you can't buy today and be covered for a storm this week — a flood-zone letter or an approaching season is a reason to act now. (Exceptions: no wait when coverage is required to close a loan, or one day after a map change puts a home in a high-risk zone.) NFIP covers up to $250,000 on the building and $100,000 on contents (contents bought separately); higher-value homes add private “excess” flood insurance. To buy: call the NFIP at 1-877-336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent — NFIP's price is set federally, so it is the same whichever agent you use.

Already flooded? Insured: start your claim with your insurer now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened; FEMA disaster aid opens only if the event gets a federal disaster declaration (FEMA individual assistance). Past aid paid here is in “Did the government pay homeowners after floods?” below.

Source: FEMA National Flood Insurance Program — waiting period, coverage limits, how to buy and how to claim, via FloodSmart.gov and FEMA.gov. Not endorsed by FEMA.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

70.5% of 7,700 single-family policies pay a premium below FEMA's own full-risk premium; the median full-risk premium is $1,618 versus a median premium charged of $966. Both are premiums only; the costs above also include fees.

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$966
  • Median full-risk premium$1,618
  • Pay below full risk70.5% of 7,700

Years to the full-risk price: under the statutory cap, premiums for most primary residences rise at most 18% a year (HFIAA cap, FEMA Risk Rating 2.0). At that maximum rate a policy at today's median premium ($966) would take at least about 4 annual renewals to reach the median full-risk price ($1,618). This is the cap on how fast a bill can climb, not a forecast of any one policy; statutory surcharges and fees are outside the cap.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Can I pay less than the sticker price?

6 of Harrison County's 6 NFIP communities carry a Community Rating System discount — a group discount a town earns for extra flood-prevention work — that cuts every eligible policy's premium, up to 20% inside the high-risk zone (Biloxi, City Of).

How much flood risk is here?

FEMA rates Harrison County's coastal flood risk Relatively High and inland flood risk Relatively Moderate — how this county compares with others, not odds for your address.

  • Coastal flood riskRelatively High
  • Inland flood riskRelatively Moderate

This is FEMA's plain risk rating for the county, a comparison — not a prediction for your home. The rating multiplies expected flood loss by a community factor for social vulnerability and resilience; the percentile below is expected loss alone, so the two can differ. Coastal: expected annual flood loss above about 87% of U.S. counties; FEMA models roughly $5,820,889 of flood loss a year across all its buildings. Inland: expected annual flood loss above about 45% of U.S. counties; FEMA models roughly $33,190,383 of flood loss a year across all its buildings. Any loss figure is a whole-county estimate across all buildings, never one home's expected loss or premium.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective NRI 2023 release; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Between 1978 and 2026, Harrison County had 15,939 NFIP flood claims, which paid $1,271,394,966 in total.

Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2005 ($1,173,324,437), 1998 ($18,242,002), 1995 ($8,587,736). Net building + contents payments by year of loss. Claims are matched by the claims dataset's county code, which may not exactly match a policy's property county.

That is 15,939 claims since 1978 against 13,404 policies in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Do flood claims here actually pay out?

Of 15,939 NFIP flood claims ever filed in Harrison County, the average paid claim came to $97,420, and 16.8% were closed with no payment.

  • Average paid claim$97,420
  • Closed with no payment16.8%
  • Claims that paid13,263

"Closed without payment" is not the same as "denied" — it includes claims below the deductible, withdrawn, or duplicate filings. Average is over claims that paid something; a single home can file across several floods over the years.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective October 25, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026. FEMA NFIP paid-claim records. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

How often has it actually flooded here?

NOAA logged 75 flood, flash-flood or coastal-flood events in Harrison County from 1996-2025, with about $3,063,000 in reported property damage.

  • Flood events logged75
  • Reported property damage$3,063,000

Physical flood events recorded by the National Weather Service for this county (1996 on), separate from insured NFIP claims — it counts floods that happened, insured or not. Damage figures are NWS field estimates, not audited, and undercount in early years.

Source: NOAA NCEI Storm Events Database. Data effective 1996-2025; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How often do the same homes flood here?

FEMA disaster-aid records show 1,454 flood-damage applications in Harrison County from homes that flooded more than once in federally declared disasters; 33 came from homes hit in four or more.

  • Repeat-flood damage records1,454
  • From homes hit 4+ times33

One home appears once for each declared disaster that damaged it, so this counts damage events on repeat-flooded homes, not distinct homes (FEMA says these records cannot be totaled by property). Disaster-aid applications since 2002, separate from NFIP insurance claims.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective October 24, 2026; retrieved October 24, 2026. FEMA Individual Assistance multiple-loss flood properties. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Did the government pay homeowners after floods?

FEMA approved $238,352,544 in Individual & Households housing help to Harrison County homeowners across 8 disasters, on 64,914 valid registrations.

FEMA Individual Assistance is disaster aid, usually capped and partial — separate from NFIP insurance and not a substitute for a policy.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA. Data effective owner registrations by disaster; retrieved October 22, 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA.

Reconciliation & data completeness

Our counts are checked against FEMA's official figure and the API's own totals.

In-force count: 13,404 policy units (from 12,068 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). FEMA official reconciliation count pending for this county. Count reconciliation (not a snapshot proof): policies: 12068/12068 fetched; claims: 15939/15939 fetched.

What this data cannot tell you

  • Your own premium — it depends on elevation, coverage and deductible. We show where existing policies fall.
  • Private (non-NFIP) flood insurance prices.
  • Your address's exact flood zone — use FEMA's Flood Map Service Center.
  • Why premiums are rising — we show the gap to full-risk, not the cause.
  • A year-over-year premium trend — the in-force snapshot holds only current-term policies, so a like-for-like multi-year index isn't possible from this data. A per-effective-year median is shown only where several years of policies exist.
